data.name: Bank of England Warns of AI Stock Bubble Risks
data.summary: Bailey cautioned that inflated AI stock prices could spark a market crash, drawing parallels to electricity and early internet investments that didn't pay off right away. Big Tech firms like Alphabet, Meta, and others face $4.49 trillion in off-balance-sheet commitments for data centers and equipment, on top of $758 billion in on-balance-sheet debt. While optimistic about AI's long-term potential, he stressed risks like cyberattacks, amid mixed market reactions and debates on whether AI will truly transform the economy soon.
data.hook: Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey sees echoes of past tech booms in today's AI hype, where big promises meet uncertain payoffs.

data.name: AI Veteran David Gilmore Launches Rayline for Open, Decentralized AI
data.summary: Gilmore, who created an early cancer detection AI still used in hundreds of U.S. hospitals and sold privacy-focused DataFleets for $100 million, announced Rayline this week. The platform uses smart model routing to slash costs by 60-90% by mixing cheaper open-source options with powerful models, aiming for more transparent and decentralized AI. After raising $8.5 million, his team plans a full launch on Wednesday, drawing praise for his ethical track record from healthcare wins to rejecting shady deals.
data.hook: David Gilmore remembers building AI in 2015 to spot cancer tumors and save lives. Now he's pushing back against big tech's money-focused shift with a new project.

data.name: Nominal Raises $240M Series C at $3B Valuation for Hardware AI Tools
data.summary: Founded four years ago by ex-defense tech experts including a former Navy submariner, Nominal builds a Hardware Intelligence Platform that unifies data across the hardware lifecycle from simulation to operations. The $240 million Series C round, led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and co-led by Insight Partners, triples its valuation to $3 billion and supports over 80 customers like Anduril and five of the seven largest defense contractors. With a recent $71 million Air Force contract and backing from Sequoia, Founders Fund, and Lockheed Martin Ventures, Nominal aims to expand into design and production while helping engineers analyze complex data in near real time.
data.hook: Hardware engineering teams have long lagged behind software speeds. Nominal is changing that with AI tools trusted by top defense players.

data.name: Archgen Labs Launches AI Tools for 3D Chip Design
data.summary: Y Combinator-backed Archgen Labs introduced tools like the Newton AI agent and LayerTherm thermal simulator to automate 3D chip physical design. These handle tasks from spotting timing issues to predicting heat maps 5,000 times faster than traditional methods, easing challenges in stacked chips that cut power use by up to 40 percent. Founders Hariharan Ayappane and Naveen Venkat aim for their first tapeout in April 2027, already partnering with GlobalFoundries. Engineers praised the speed and automation in early reactions.
data.hook: Building semiconductor chips like skyscrapers means stacking transistors vertically to pack more power into smaller spaces. Archgen Labs just unveiled AI agents to make that stacking faster and smarter.

data.name: Skild AI Open-Sources Steel Physics Solver for Faster Robot Training
data.summary: Steel, built with NVIDIA and integrated into the open-source Newton Physics Engine, tackles bottlenecks in robotic manipulation by delivering up to 13 times the throughput of PhysX on mixed tasks while using less GPU memory. Skild CEO Deepak Pathak highlighted how it pairs with AI-generated environments to speed up training for contact-heavy jobs like cable handling. NVIDIA complemented the launch at CoRL 2026 with GR00T 2, an open humanoid model, and Isaac Lab 3.0 updates, fueling community excitement for bridging simulation to real robots. Developers can now test Steel in browsers and contribute on GitHub.
data.hook: Skild AI just released Steel, a lightning-fast physics engine that cranks robot simulations to 3.9 million steps per second—making it easier to teach machines real-world skills like grasping and handling objects.
